lesson_title: Launch and diagnostic: requirements and decomposition
standards: Michigan Computer Science: Algorithms and Programming

materials: unit-specific source, model, manipulatives, safe materials, or approved digital tool
task_brief: Day 1 of "Programming and Software Design" (unit 2, grade 8) is a diagnostic probe on requirements and decomposition. It is one step inside the unit — not the whole unit project — and takes about 40–60 minutes. The unit is working toward: Build a small application, simulation, or game that solves a defined user need. Today's work contributes to that by handling requirements and decomposition at the launch and diagnostic stage, against the unit's wider topics of requirements and decomposition, data and variables, selection and iteration, and functions or procedures. This session is formative: it is scored on completeness and honesty of the record, not on getting a polished result.
primary_task: Before any explanation of requirements and decomposition, record what you already think. Write your current best answer to how requirements and decomposition works, then sketch — in words, boxes, or pseudocode — the steps you believe are involved. Predict one input that would make your sketch fail. Then run or hand-trace your own sketch against two inputs you invent and mark where the prediction held and where it broke. Wrong predictions are the point of this task and cost you nothing; an unrecorded prediction is the only way to lose credit. The activity_setup block below supplies the complete central input, exact specification, execution method, test cases, debugging target, and equal-credit manual simulation; use those exact materials rather than waiting for another handout, account, service, or tool. Anchor today's work inside its unit: this session's evidence is about requirements and decomposition, and it belongs to "Programming and Software Design", which also covers separate topics such as data and variables. Close out with this check before you stop: In one concise response, show or explain the most important idea about requirements and decomposition; then identify one check that would catch an error or weak claim. At grade 8 the bar is independent work that anticipates the obvious objection: name the case most likely to break your result, test it, and report what happened.
requirements: Meet this lesson's own success criteria: The learner completes the central task about requirements and decomposition., The learner gives evidence, reasoning, a model, or a documented process rather than an unsupported answer., and The learner checks or revises the work and can identify a next step.
Address the lesson objective: Activate prior knowledge about requirements and decomposition, surface initial thinking without penalty, and establish the unit question.
Produce the deliverable for a diagnostic probe: Dated prediction sheet, first-attempt sketch or pseudocode, and a two-input trace showing where the prediction held and broke.
Show the process, not only the result — a trace, test log, draft trail, or commit history.
Complete the check criteria list in this package before submitting.
deliverable: Dated prediction sheet, first-attempt sketch or pseudocode, and a two-input trace showing where the prediction held and broke.

central_input.title: Inline requirements and decomposition code case
central_input.purpose: Use this exact fictional case to investigate requirements and decomposition; no other file, model, dataset, or account is needed.

expected_behavior_and_specification: The procedure must execute every supplied step in order; the main input must return open > check > save.
An empty step list must return an empty string, and a one-step list must retain that step.
The submitted explanation must connect the observed control flow or data state to requirements and decomposition, not merely state the final number.
The boundary test must be completed and its actual result compared explicitly with the expected result.

execution_method.primary: No-install browser method: open any browser developer console, paste the complete starter code, press Enter, and record the output or exact error text.
execution_method.local_optional: If Node.js is already installed, save the unchanged snippet as activity.js and run `node activity.js`; installing Node.js is not required.
execution_method.no_computer_required: The hand-trace route below is a complete execution method and earns identical credit.

debugging_target.observed_failure: The main input should retain all three steps, but the unchanged program returns check > save.
debugging_target.target: Use the specification, unchanged run, and test table to locate the first divergent state or control-flow decision; explain the evidence before choosing an edit.
debugging_target.pre_attempt_support: Before editing, record the unchanged output and identify which stated rule is first contradicted. Do not look for or request a finished repair.
debugging_target.scope_note: Diagnosing the state, control-flow, or data defect and connecting the repair to requirements and decomposition is the central evidence.

equal_credit_alternative.method: Paper or notes-app simulation; this earns exactly the same score as running code.
steps: Make one row for each statement or loop check and copy the starting input exactly.
Record every variable, object field, selected item, and output after that step.
Circle the first row where the actual state stops matching the specification.
Apply the one repair named in your explanation and trace all three tests again.
equal_credit_alternative.evidence_to_submit: The completed trace, the one-line corrected condition, and an expected-versus-actual table for all three tests.

test_or_check_criteria: A written prediction about requirements and decomposition exists and is dated before any instruction or reference was consulted.
At least two self-chosen inputs were traced against the initial sketch, with the outcome of each recorded.
Each place the prediction held and each place it broke is marked explicitly rather than silently corrected.
No real account, password, API key, or live system was used — all inputs are invented or sandboxed.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: Everything in this task runs in a sandbox or on paper. Never use a real password, passphrase, API key, account credential, access token, precise home location, or any real person's identifiable information — invent fictional values instead. Do not sign into, probe, scan, stress, or attempt access to any live, production, school, or third-party system, and do not bypass a filter, licence, access control, or terms of service. Any practice login used in an example must be obviously invented — a silly made-up name paired with a nonsense multi-word phrase — and must never be anything you or anyone in your family actually uses somewhere real. If a task seems to need something real, substitute a made-up stand-in and note the substitution.

copyright_and_authorship: The graded submission must be your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI tool may explain an idea, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but must not produce, write, debug, or make any part of the work that is scored. Any code, asset, or text you did not write must be openly licensed or supplied for this task, and must be cited in a comment or note naming where it came from and what you changed.

task_accessibility_provisions: Provide a screen-reader-compatible editor, adjustable font size and contrast, and a complete keyboard-only workflow. An offline paper-and-trace route is available for every task here and is scored identically to an on-screen one.
Breaks, extended time, a hidden timer, reduced copying, and a low-distraction setting are available on request and never reduce the score.
safety_and_privacy_rules: Allow a pause, break, or alternate response mode without treating it as failure.
Never require a real password, private message, precise location, account credential, or identifiable image.
Use approved sites and tools; do not bypass filters, access controls, licensing, or terms of service.
Treat AI output as a draft to verify, not as an authority or a substitute for learner work.

media.suggestion: Optional diagram, map, worked example, source image, demonstration, or short clip supporting requirements and decomposition.
media.fallback: Provide the same information as readable steps, alt text, transcript, tactile/concrete model, or teacher demonstration.

remediation: Reteaching for requirements and decomposition follows the signal actually observed, not a fixed script. If the signal is "prerequisite gap": Return to the smallest prerequisite needed for requirements and decomposition, model it with a concrete or text-only representation, then retry one fresh item. If the signal is "procedure without understanding": Ask the learner to explain or represent why the process for requirements and decomposition works before continuing. If the signal is "correct but low confidence": Confirm the reasoning specifically, offer one varied example of requirements and decomposition, and avoid unnecessary remediation. If the signal is "repeated error pattern": Name the observable pattern neutrally, contrast it with a worked example, and schedule a short same-day or next-session review. If the signal is "mastery evidence": Require accurate independent application plus explanation on a later or different occasion before marking requirements and decomposition mastered. Re-check with one fresh item of the same kind before moving on, and record which signal was seen so the pattern is visible across the unit rather than treated as a one-off.
extension: Apply requirements and decomposition under a new constraint, compare two approaches or perspectives, or teach the idea with an original example without completing another learner’s graded work. Treat this as optional depth on requirements and decomposition rather than extra volume: one harder case done well beats three more of the same. Extension work stays inside the same sandbox rules — no real credentials and no live external systems. Extension work is never required to reach mastery and must not be assigned as a penalty.
